xref.title: Performing During Woodstock 99 Fires (1999)
xref.body: The Red Hot Chili Peppers took the stage at Woodstock 99 on Sunday night amidst a growing mob mentality and escalating violence. A peace group had distributed 100,000 candles for a vigil during their set, but the unruly crowd used these candles to set fires, looting vendor booths, burning plywood walls, and even toppling a speaker tower. The situation was further exacerbated when the band launched into their cover of Jimi Hendrix's "Fire," which seemingly encouraged more arson. "it was probably a really bad idea for the chili peppers to launch into their cover of Jimmy Hendrix's fire, which of course only encouraged more fire."

xref.title: Accidental Recording of Piss Factory
xref.body: The recording of "Piss Factory" was somewhat accidental. Patti Smith and Lenny Kay had booked studio time to record a cover of the Jimi Hendrix song "Hey Joe," but they finished early. With the remaining time, they recorded "Piss Factory," a track that recounted Smith's experiences working in a doll factory. "Piss Factory was sort of an accident. They had booked time to record a cover of the Jimmy Hendrix song Hey Joe and finished early."

xref.title: Early Influences
xref.body: While growing up and playing in local bands, Neil Peart was deeply influenced by prominent drummers across different genres. He admired Keith Moon of The Who, Ginger Baker of Cream, John Bonham of Led Zeppelin, and Mitch Mitchell of The Jimi Hendrix Experience. Additionally, he was fascinated by big band drummers such as Gene Krupa and Buddy Rich. "He loved Keith Moon of the Who, ginger baker of cream, John Bonham of Zeppelin, and Mitch Mitchell of Jimmy Hendrix's groove."

xref.title: Early Influences and Musical Development
xref.body: Jeff Buckley, born to Tim Buckley and Mary Guibert, met his father only once. His mother was a classically trained musician, while his stepfather introduced him to bands like Pink Floyd, Jimi Hendrix, The Who, Led Zeppelin, and Queen. Jeff picked up the guitar at age 5, discovered Rush, Kiss, and various prog rock bands, and received his first electric guitar at age 12. "One of the people Tim left behind was his eight-year-old son, Jeff, who admitted his father only once. Mom was a classically trained musician playing piano and cello. Meanwhile, Jeff's death father was into Pink Floyd, Jimmy Hendrix, the who led Zeppelin and Queen. He picked up a guitar at age 5, discovered rush and kiss and various prog rock bands, which led to his first electric guitar at age 12."

xref.title: The Log's Recording and Companion Instrument
xref.body: A recording made in 1948 features "the log" along with another experimental instrument called "the Clunker." The Clunker was an old hollow-body guitar modified with a hole in the back, allowing Les Paul to easily access and "lobotomize" its internal electronics, effectively making it a playable workbench. "OK, that's not exactly Jimmy Hendrix, but again, that recording was made in 1948. We hear the log on that track, along with another monster called the Clunker, which was an old hollow body with a hole in the back that allowed Les Paul to lobotomize all the electronics inside. It was like a workbench you could play."
